units: the smell of the damp material reaches the visitor before anything else
a fine dust covers the floor of the room
the fast spinning of the wheel is the cause of that dust
unfired vessels pile up on the shelves
their greyish tint will change once they have been through the kiln
the presence of the kiln speeds up the drying of the pieces
the craftsman therefore protects some pieces with a wet cloth
the walls have never been given any paint
every object set down in the workshop serves a practical purpose
text: Push the workshop door open and the damp clay strikes you before anything else, a persistent smell settling at the back of the throat. Fine dust lies right across the floorboards, thrown off the wheel whenever it picks up speed. The shelves sag under unfired bowls, a dull greyish colour that will warm considerably once they have come out of the kiln. That kiln stands at the far end of the room, and because it stands there the heat climbs and dries the pottery much faster than the potter would like, so he keeps a soaked cloth spread over the pieces still awaiting their turn. The walls are rough and have never seen a coat of paint. Stay an hour and the arrangement becomes obvious: nothing here is decorative. Every tool on the workbench has earned its place by performing a task.

units: the closing of a venue happens in successive stages
the usual explanation blames the public for drifting away
the crowds at neighbouring stages contradict that explanation
the level of rent swallows the margin left by the takings
a first solution is to share technical costs between venues
those venues wrongly take one another for rivals
a second solution rests on leases of long duration
that guarantee demands in return affordable prices and original work given a stage
text: A theatre does not shut its doors in one go. It fades away by stages, a season cut short, a subscription put on hold, a technical crew reduced to a handful. The usual verdict blames audiences for drifting away, yet the queues outside the stages down the road make that lazy reading rather hard to defend. The real squeeze is rent, which swallows whatever margin the box office still manages to return. Two remedies exist, and neither of them calls for a miracle. The first is to share the heavy costs, sets, lighting desks and insurance, between houses that take each other for rivals while courting one and the same public. The second is to secure long leases, granted against a plain undertaking: affordable seats, and original work given a stage. Otherwise we shall go on mourning closures that we arranged ourselves.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a specialist repairs old paintings
her manner recalls that of a woman who repairs watches
both trades call for tiny movements repeated again and again
she lifts the darkened varnish with a swab of cotton
she halts her hand as soon as the tint underneath turns doubtful
the material of a movement answers in a predictable way
a painting instead sets against her old retouching and deposits of smoke
the aim of the woman who repairs watches is to start the object again
the aim of the specialist is to keep the painter's hand legible
text: The woman who mends old paintings leans over her canvas much the way a watch repairer leans over a movement that has stopped. Both trades live off the same small motions, made again and again, and neither of them forgives a slip. She lifts the darkened varnish a thumbnail at a time, with cotton wound round the end of a stick, and her arm halts the moment the colour underneath turns uncertain. The watch repairer straightens a wheel that a knock has bent, and the metal answers her plainly, while paint argues back with old retouching and with layers dulled by the smoke of lamps. What parts the two of them is the aim. One wants the machine running again. The other wants nothing at all to run: she asks only that some later eye should still read what a hand laid down there, one evening, on stretched cloth.

units: the exhibition shows prints
the deep inks do not fill in the dark areas
the paper used has a coarse texture
that texture softens the contrast of the light surfaces
the order of hanging follows the successive states of the plates
that arrangement makes the progress of the engraved drawing visible
the labels lack any indication of the technique used
that absence hampers the unversed visitor
text: Three things go right in this hanging of prints, and one thing goes wrong. Take the inking first: the blacks hold their depth without ever filling in the hollows, so that the finest lines keep their air and several plates take on a startling relief. Then the support, a paper of coarse grain, almost felted under the finger, which softens the whites and stops the contrast from turning harsh. Then the sequence: the plates hang by successive states, and the visitor watches the composition assemble itself, from an unfinished sketch through to the settled version. The lapse lies in the labels, silent on process, on tool, on the bite of the acid. A practised eye will rebuild the method unaided; whoever meets this field for the first time leaves with a vague admiration and nothing whatever learnt.

units: the writer thanks the woman who ran an etching course
he came to the workshop with no previous experience
the first session dealt with the preparation of the plates
he then learnt to control how long the bite lasts
one of his plates was ruined during a trial
the woman in charge offered him a fresh start straight away
the last session yielded a successful impression
the writer wishes to enrol on the following course
text: I am writing at the close of the etching course that you led, in order to thank you for it. I came to the workshop with no practice whatever, and rather uneasy about holding a needle among participants who plainly knew their trade. The opening session, given over to degreasing and grounding the plates, settled that worry at once: your instructions were spare and exact, and nobody in the room was left behind. We moved on to the control of the bite, and I understood that the time spent in the bath decides very nearly everything. My second plate was spoilt by an excess of acid; you invited me straight away to prepare another, without a word of reproach. The final session yielded a clean impression, of which I am proud. I should therefore like to enrol on the next course, if any places remain.

units: an engineer explains how old recordings are put back in order
the hiss comes from the wear of the original carrier
excessive filtering also wipes out useful sound
the top notes of the string instruments go first
the engineer therefore prefers a measured correction
he compares several copies of the same recording
that comparison serves to tell an isolated fault from a shared one
he always keeps an unaltered version of the file
text: People often ask the sound engineer where the veil over old recordings comes from. His answer runs to a single sentence: the carrier has worn, and the wear adds a steady hiss that no microphone ever picked up. Can it be taken out altogether? He says not, or rather that it should not be, because heavy filtering carries off the highest harmonics of the strings along with the hiss, and the sound goes flat. What does he do instead? He applies a restrained correction, and then compares several copies of the same disc: a crackle found on one copy belongs to that copy alone, and a crackle found on every one of them belongs to the cutting itself. One rule governs the whole business. The original is archived untouched, since a judgement made by ear yesterday may well look wrong tomorrow.

units: an actress reports a sound problem to a stage manager
her voice becomes inaudible at the back of the house
the stage manager first assumes a failure of the microphone
the wooden set is in fact throwing the sound back towards the stage
a thick rug is laid on the floor to soak up those reflections
the speakers are turned towards the distant seats
the actress checks the result from the last row
the difficulty disappears at the very next rehearsal
text: The actress caught the stage manager at the edge of the platform and told him that nobody past the third row could make her out any more. He said the microphone must be fading, that he would swap the battery over and they would see. She pushed back: the trouble started earlier, before the microphone came into it at all, because the boarded set threw her own voice straight back at her and made her force it. He granted that she was right, then offered a thick rug at the foot of the panel to swallow those returns. After that they tilted the speakers towards the back rows, which had been sitting in a dead patch. She went off to listen from there while an understudy read her line, and came back saying that it was clear at last. At the next run nobody craned forward to catch the words.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two old ways of fixing images are set against each other
wall painting addresses a large public
the decorated manuscript is meant for a single reader
wall painting is carried out quickly on plaster that is still wet
the illuminator may break off and take up his work whenever he likes
wall painting has suffered from changes in the use of buildings
manuscripts have survived better because they were stored out of harm
both techniques used comparable pigments
text: Two ways of fixing an image ran side by side for a long stretch, and they differ on almost every count. Wall painting speaks to a crowd: it takes a whole face of stone, reads from a distance, and presses its figures on anyone who steps through the door. The decorated page is meant for a single reader, bent close over it, turning the leaf at his own pace. Part of the gap comes from the craft itself. Wet plaster grants the painter one sitting and no more, which rules out second thoughts and demands a sure line; the illuminator shuts his volume and takes the work up again whenever he pleases. Their fates parted too. Walls were whitewashed, cut through and put to other uses as buildings changed hands, while volumes shelved in a locked press came down whole. The pigments came from the same grindings.

units: the colouring matter used in painting has three distinct origins
the first origin is mineral and comes from crushed rock
those mineral powders hold their tint for a long time
the second origin is vegetable and comes from roots or berries
vegetable colours grow pale under a strong light
the third origin comes from insects or shells
these last were rare and costly
a binder turns the coloured powder into a usable paste
text: Three families of colour share the painter's palette, and each of them carries the story of where it came from. The first is quarried: a stone is crushed, the powder sifted, and out of it comes a deep blue or a warm ochre that will hold for ages without weakening, for rock keeps no memory of the light that falls on it. The second rises from plants, from roots torn up, from berries pressed, from wood left to steep; these tints are airy, almost floating, lovely at first glance, yet they grow pale under a strong light and end as shadows of themselves. The third comes from living creatures, from gathered shells and dried insects, and its scarcity kept it for lavish commissions. One gesture is common to all: powder is nothing until a binder takes it up and makes a workable paste of it.

units: a tuner works on an instrument before a concert
the hall was too warm when he arrived
the heat had slackened the strings unevenly
he first set a reference note against the fork
he then adjusted the other notes by successive fifths
a bass string gave way during the operation
he replaced that string and then stretched it by hand
he measured the temperature before checking a second time
text: The tuner walked into the hall a full hour before the concert and judged the air too warm from the doorway itself. The heat had slackened the stringing unevenly, the bass having shifted a good deal more than the middle register. He began by setting a reference note against the fork, by ear, with no device at all, then worked upward in fifths, narrowing each interval by a beat that he counted off. The going was rough: on the third pass a bass string snapped outright, and the wire coiled itself across the soundboard. He laid in a fresh one, seated it firmly on its anchor, and stretched it by hand so that it would settle before the players arrived. Then, with a thermometer to hand, he waited for the air to come down, and took the whole tuning again from the very first note.
